summary: Huron sits on the dead-flat western floor of the San Joaquin Valley, surrounded by irrigated row crops and nut orchards that stretch unbroken to the horizon in every direction — a place where the sky is enormous and the nearest incorporated city of any size, Coalinga, is about twenty miles northwest. At just 1.7 square miles, the entire town is compact enough to cross on foot, but there's essentially no commercial variety to walk to; grocery and dining options are minimal, and any serious retail trip means driving to Fresno, roughly sixty miles east on State Route 198. The economy is almost entirely agricultural — packing houses, field operations, and related services are the dominant employers — which means work is local but seasonal, and switching jobs without a long commute is difficult outside that single industry. A median home value of $236,500 against a median household income of around $44,800 yields a price-to-income ratio above 5:1, and with a poverty rate exceeding 33%, even modest rents near $1,060 consume a significant share of earnings. Summers are punishing, with average daytime highs well into the 80s and frequent triple-digit spikes, though nearly ten hours of daily sunshine year-round keeps winter mild. School performance data shows ELA and math scores more than 100 points below state standards, and the bachelor's-degree attainment rate of 2.5% is among the lowest of any incorporated place in California. Huron is, in the most literal sense, a company town — except the company is an entire industry, and the town's fortunes rise and fall with the valley's water supply.
